title: Nobody Improves in One Saturday
author: Fantastic Maths
summary: A maths department head reflects on his third year attending researchED National, structuring the piece around two specific sessions -- Sam Crome's on applying cognitive science principles (retrieval, cognitive load management) to staff teams rather than just students, and Adam Robbins's reframing of teacher motivation research to argue competence and relatedness, not autonomy alone, are the more reliable drivers of engagement. His most transferable synthesis is noticing these two sessions meet: a department that returns to the same core ideas over time, using retrieval to revisit them, gives staff both the shared direction (relatedness) and the visible sense of demonstrable improvement (competence) that motivation research suggests actually moves people, without requiring leaders to hand over the open-ended autonomy that instinct usually reaches for first. The essay's most self-aware section confronts an uncomfortable possibility directly: since his school's existing practice already aligns closely with what researchED's mainstream sessions recommend, is that evidence the work has genuinely landed, or is it the exact moment confirmation bias becomes dangerous? His answer is a deliberate selection rule -- attending sessions from speakers he's broadly aware of but rarely actually hears, rather than the voices already in his ears -- treated not merely as a way to manage an overwhelming conference program but as a small, intentional mechanism for being nudged rather than confirmed. He also credits sending 20-30 staff across all roles (not just teachers) for three consecutive years with producing shared reference points across the school, rather than one person's notes that nobody else reads.
points: The essay's key synthesis links two separate conference sessions into one actionable practice: applying cognitive-science principles (retrieval, cognitive load) to staff development, combined with building visible, demonstrable competence rather than granting open-ended autonomy, together supply the competence and relatedness that motivation research shows drive engagement more reliably than autonomy alone.

The reframing of teacher motivation as a continuum (extrinsic moving toward intrinsic) rather than a binary opposition directly challenges the common leadership instinct to hand a struggling colleague more autonomy, arguing a well-constructed menu of approaches with visible progress may be the better form of support, not a lesser one.

The essay's most intellectually honest move is treating 'we already do everything researchED recommends' as a genuinely ambiguous signal rather than pure validation -- naming explicitly that it could equally mean the work has landed or that confirmation bias has taken hold, and building a deliberate selection rule (avoid familiar voices) specifically to guard against the latter.

Sending 20-30 staff across all roles (not just teachers) to the same conference for three consecutive years is credited with producing shared reference points that survive better than a single attendee's notes, directly linking conference attendance policy to durable whole-school culture change.
quotes: What researchED is for isn't handing anyone a rulebook. It's moving the profession, collectively and slowly, towards being more evidence-informed than it was last year. My own word for that is nudge.
And with it came a warning: A senior leader runs the whole-school session on cognitive load; their middle leaders then run team meetings that do the precise opposite of everything that session said.
The takeaway I'm still chewing on: building competence, and letting people see their own development, is a bigger driver than whether they arrived at the solution entirely under their own steam.
Read generously, it's evidence the work has genuinely landed. Read critically, it's the exact moment confirmation bias becomes the danger.
Avoiding the voices already in my ears isn't just a way of managing an overwhelming programme. It's a small, deliberate attempt to be nudged rather than confirmed.
Three years in, we've stopped only consuming this thing and started contributing to it.
